CRM WORKSPACE UI REVIEW · 4 NOVEMBER 2026
01 / Decision summary

Make the interface consistent before adding more decoration

Your CRM already supports the main time-tracking and administration workflows. The next UI update should make those workflows easier to scan and act on: consistent headings, predictable cards, clear action priority and less space between a user and the control they need.

Recommended direction: retain the green workspace identity and existing permissions, calculations and timer rules. Build a shared component standard, then apply it to the most frequently used screens. This is a UI report, not an instruction to replace the app or its backend.

First prioritiesWhy they matter
One header and toolbar patternTasks currently repeats its page heading; other modules use different title treatments.
One card family with clear purposesMetric, navigation, team selection and editing cards need different, predictable behavior.
Readable, quieter controlsSecondary text is often small, and too many toolbar actions compete with Save or Create.
Shorter paths to useful contentRepeated context bars, tall headers and stacked filters reduce the number of visible rows.
Consistent mobile and keyboard behaviorPinned controls, horizontal tables and floating theme controls need careful focus and overlap checks.

Evidence: current source, fresh synthetic-data captures of six administration modules and two forms, and existing 4 November QA captures for hours, links, reports and desktop states. No production employee records were used. This is an expert review, not a measured usability study or a WCAG certification.

03 / Layout and navigation

Give more of the screen to the work

FindingRecommendationPriority
F01 · Duplicate and inconsistent titlesRender one page title. Use one compact title / description / primary-action row across lists and settings.P1
F02 · Repeated vertical contextKeep breadcrumb and title. Make the generic date/context line and footer less prominent on dense work screens.P1
F03 · Group expansion is not visually explicitAdd a chevron and clear expanded state to sidebar group headings. Keep the current group open and preserve keyboard activation.P2
F04 · Different type identitiesChoose one application heading family. Current shared pages use Georgia while newer hours settings use sans-serif.P1

Recommended page structure

Breadcrumb → compact page header → filters → results → context-specific footer. Keep Save with the editor and Create with the list header. Do not add an introductory launch card before an editor that the navigation already opens directly.

The existing collapsible sidebar and route search are useful. Avoid replacing them with extra decorative navigation cards on every page. Use team cards where selecting a team is the actual first step, as in Working Hours.

04 / Card design

Use a small family of cards with clear behavior

Cards should communicate a purpose, not merely add white boxes. Keep a consistent radius, border, title style and spacing, then vary the internal layout according to what the card does.

Card typeRequired contentInteraction
MetricLabel, value, unit, time scope, optional comparisonRead-only unless a specific drilldown is provided; label that drilldown.
Team selectionTeam icon, name, member count, configuration countEntire card opens the team; show hover, focus and selected state.
Employee selectionName, employee ID, team, relevant statusClear checkbox or selection control; separate individual Edit action.
ProgressCompleted / required, percentage, pending, overtimeCaption explains the denominator; use a real progress value.
EditorSection title, scope summary, fields, feedback, SaveKeep the primary action visible and protect unsaved changes.
Report / list containerTitle, result count, filters or tableUse rows for comparison; avoid putting every table cell into a card.

Proposed visual examples

PROPOSED COMPONENT STANDARD · Illustrative values, not application data
WCPA

11 employees · 9 configured

Open employees
Required hours today
40h of 5 present employees

27h completed · 13h pending

  • Use 16-20 px internal padding, 12 px corners and a subtle 1 px border as the proposed baseline. These are design targets, not current measured values.
  • Reserve elevation for menus, dialogs and pinned controls. A shadow on every nested panel adds noise.
  • Use the same selected treatment everywhere: accent border plus a check or text state. Hover alone must not look selected.
  • Avoid whole-card buttons containing nested action buttons. A team card can open details; employee Edit and checkbox controls need distinct targets.

F05 · Progress meaning: the existing activity card bar scales hours against the busiest team; the new productivity bar measures requirement completion. Similar bars imply the same meaning. Label or restyle them so a relative-hours bar cannot be read as a percentage target.

05 / Icons and visual tokens

Standardize icons typography and color

Lucide is already used by the web shell and several modules. Keep that family; a larger icon collection is not the main need. Make meaning, weight and placement consistent. The mapping below is a proposed design vocabulary.

IconMeaningIconMeaning
OverviewTeams and people
ClientsProjects
TasksRelationships and links
Tracked timeAdd manual entry
EditBilling
Date and attendanceSettings
SearchExpand / collapse
BreakWarning or attention
DeleteExport or download

Proposed type and spacing scale

  • Body 14 px; supporting labels 12 px; page title 24-28 px; card title 16 px; KPI 28-32 px.
  • Use tabular numerals for clocks, hours, rates and totals. Keep seconds when editing or reconciling time.
  • Use 4 / 8 / 12 / 16 / 24 / 32 px spacing tokens instead of one-off margins.

Proposed icon and color rules

  • 16 px inside controls, 20 px in cards, consistent stroke weight around 1.75-2.
  • Brand green for primary actions; neutral for secondary; red for destructive confirmation; amber for warnings.
  • Use text labels with unfamiliar icons. Give icon-only controls accessible names and adequate hit areas.

F06 · Small labels: shared styles include 10-11 px supporting text. Do not assume that every small label fails accessibility; prioritize frequently read names, scope notes and form help for enlargement.

F07 · Theme governance: nine theme definitions exist and the default is Console blue. Saved Upsilon green is preserved. Choose a primary review theme and test one alternate; maintain identical geometry and semantic status meaning across palettes. The desktop installer also uses the default Electron icon: add a branded app icon as a separate asset task.

06 / Forms and actions

Make editing clearer without changing business rules

FindingProposed change
F08 · Required markers create extra linesKeep the label and required indicator inline. Group related fields; make optional sections visibly optional.
F09 · Unequal form treatmentUse a shared Field, Select, MultiSelect and FormSection standard with consistent spacing, help, validation and disabled states.
F10 · Too many actions use primary stylingOne dominant action per active editor. Search, Refresh, Clear and Back should normally be neutral; reserve brand fill for Save / Create / Start.
F11 · Long forms need progressive disclosureKeep account identity first; expand rates or other optional sections only when needed. Preserve the currently useful sticky action footer.

Relationships and destructive changes

Keep one project selection section for task creation/editing and preserve multiple-project support. In linking and entry corrections, show exactly which teams, projects, clients and employees will change before confirmation. Use explicit button labels such as Confirm unlink; display success only after the server confirms it.

Move from class-name-based button styling toward explicit Primary, Secondary, Tertiary and Destructive variants. The shared stylesheet currently changes appearance by matching words in CSS class names, which makes a new button’s appearance harder to predict.

07 / Tables and reports

Improve scanning before adding more charts

FindingProposed changePriority
F12 · Search inset collisionPlace the icon in a fixed slot; reserve padding before text in every size. Recheck focus and typed text.P1
F13 · Wide tables hide useful actionsPrioritize employee/task name, status and the main action. Put lower-frequency fields in details or a column chooser.P1
F14 · Table controls vary by moduleStandardize search placement, filter labels, page size, sort indicators and pagination. Keep the result count near the table.P2
F15 · Duration formats vary by purposeUse concise hours/minutes in summaries; show seconds in detailed records, corrections and audit evidence. Label timezone and date scope.P1
F16 · Overloaded report landing viewsStart with the relevant team/employee scope. Keep grouping and exports near the report, not in a separate decorative card.P2

Recommended table anatomy: title and count → compact filters → column headings → records → pagination. Pin identity or actions only when needed. Keep one clear horizontal scroll region; a page that fits the viewport can still contain an intentionally scrollable table.

For mobile, show the person or task, status and main action first; expand contact, rates and secondary fields on demand. The current employee mobile view stacks each field into a tall section, so one record can consume most of a screen. This is responsive, but not yet efficient for reviewing a team.

08 / Hours and linking workflows

Keep the recent improvements and make scope unmistakable

Working hours

  • Keep the team cards, Whole team / Choose employees actions and individual Edit requirement flow. These improvements are already implemented.
  • F17 · Show the active team and selected employee count beside Save. When a search hides selected members, state that those members are still selected. Whole team should explicitly mean all members, not only visible rows.
  • F18 · Differentiate daily target, half-day percentage and approved date exception. Show a duration preview beside decimal input; preserve 7.8 hours = 7h 48m.
  • Keep pending and overtime separate. For unconfigured or zero-requirement staff, consider an em dash or Not configured / No requirement instead of an unexplained 0% progress bar.

Task links and project and client links

  • Keep the two independent routes and their distinct scopes. The client-only page must not require task selection.
  • F19 · Make the selection summary the review anchor: Projects × Clients × Tasks, selected names, and action. Keep link and unlink review wording distinct.
  • Keep successful-save reset and History below the editor. A history list is completed actions, not necessarily a complete inventory of current links; label that distinction.
  • A fixed-height picker is useful for long catalogs. On smaller laptops, reduce header padding before reducing row readability or hiding review actions.

Business meaning to preserve: productive tracked time is not task completion. Leave, half-day targets, client-specific task access and historical time must retain their existing rules throughout any visual update.

09 / Desktop and mobile

Make state and the next action easy to understand

AreaRecommendation
F20 · Timer statesKeep Not started, Starting, Working, On break, Idle and connection-error states distinct. Use the server-confirmed timer; never show speculative elapsed work.
F21 · Continue versus StartThe idle acknowledgement does not restart the timer. Consider Return to CRM or a short explicit note so Continue is not mistaken for Resume work.
F22 · Settings copy versus real behaviorThe captured idle settings page says Pause a running timer, while the current desktop idle flow stops work. Update wording to the actual policy rather than changing behavior to match old text.
F23 · Desktop startup and lockKeep CRM visible above the blank overlay, explain why the screen is covered, and unlock only after confirmed Start. Include a clear connection-recovery message.
F24 · Mobile efficiencyUse compact identity rows, collapsible secondary details and reachable actions. Pinned controls must leave enough viewport for the record being selected.

Keep native desktop controls distinct from browser administration. The timer screen should prioritize the chosen project/client/task, truthful status, elapsed time and Start/Stop. An administrative card dashboard is not a replacement for that focused timer workflow.

Compare interaction patterns rather than copy a whole product

The comparison uses official documentation accessed on 4 November 2026. These are documented patterns and design references, not hands-on paid-account audits, feature-parity claims or ratings of the entire products. Availability can vary by role and plan.

ReferenceDocumented patternWhat to adapt for CRMWhat to verify yourself
Handdy [R1]Desktop time capture and website reports organized around clients, projects, tasks and teams.Clear capture-versus-reporting roles, consistent scope filters and explicit work/break labels.Try the current timer and report interface. Do not infer present visual quality from help text.
Clockify [R2] [R3]Personal/team dashboard contexts; team activity table; summary, detailed and weekly reports.Clear person/team context, task-oriented report modes and optional prominence for frequently used activity data.Run the same report task in both apps; compare filter effort, row readability and drilldown.
Hubstaff [R4]Dashboard widgets can be managed, moved or removed; personal and team contexts are separated.Give managers a short, relevant overview and clearly scoped widgets. Start with a sensible fixed layout before adding customization.Check which metrics employees actually need; do not add widgets only to fill space.

Dense records may still work better in a list.

Recommended reference mix

Clockify: report organization. Hubstaff: overview relevance. ClickUp: reusable card concepts. Handdy: the desktop-to-web workflow that your employees already recognize. Your existing green brand, team access rules and Upsilon defaults can remain your own.

Do not treat screenshots from different screen sizes or themes as a fair comparison. Match the viewport, role, date range, sample size and task first. Use the worksheet on page 13 to collect comparable evidence.

11 / Accessibility and feedback

Validate readability and recovery in every state

This review identifies risks and proposes checks; it does not establish WCAG conformance. Small text, a cropped screenshot or an icon alone is not sufficient evidence of a formal failure.

CheckAcceptance target for the update
Text contrast [R6]Measure actual foreground/background pairs. WCAG AA requires 4.5:1 for ordinary text and 3:1 for qualifying large text. Check muted help text and every theme.
Pointer targets [R7]WCAG 2.2 AA target-size criterion is 24 × 24 CSS px, with defined exceptions including spacing. Use 40-44 px as a practical product target for frequent touch controls; that larger target is a recommendation.
Visible keyboard focus [R8]Tab through menus, filters, rows, drawers and pinned controls. Focus must not be entirely hidden by author-created content. Prefer fully visible focus.
Icons and labelsGive icon-only controls accessible names. Use adjacent text for status; do not rely on green/red alone. Keep decorative icons out of the accessibility tree.
DialogsKeep the existing ModalFrame focus trap, Escape handling and focus return. Verify long forms and custom dropdowns inside each dialog, not only the shell.
Motion and refreshRespect reduced-motion preferences. Background refresh should not steal focus, reset selections or erase unsaved notes.

Feedback states to standardize

StateExpected treatment
Initial loadingShort status or skeleton with a stable layout; do not present a meaningful zero before data arrives.
Empty resultsDistinguish no records, no matches and no access. Offer the relevant next step.
SavingDisable duplicate submission, state which action is pending, and preserve context.
SuccessConfirm the saved scope. Reset fields only where the existing workflow requires it.
Validation or stale updateKeep selections, explain what must change, and offer reload/retry without claiming the save succeeded.
Network failureShow the last successful result when available and label it as stale. Keep a clear retry action.

F25 · Floating theme control: screenshots show it occupying the bottom-right region near row actions and panel footers. Move it into an account/settings menu, or reserve space so it cannot obscure an actionable control.

12 / Update priorities

A practical backlog for a controlled UI refresh

Priority reflects likely frequency and user impact, not a measured defect count. Effort is relative: S = isolated component or copy, M = several related screens, L = shared structure with broader regression testing. No delivery dates are implied.

PriorityWork itemEvidenceEffort
P1Remove duplicate Tasks heading; adopt one compact page header.F01, F02, F04S-M
P1Fix employee search icon/text inset at desktop and mobile sizes.F12S
P1Correct idle stop/pause and acknowledgement wording.F21, F22S
P1Make primary/secondary/destructive button variants explicit.F10, F16M
P1Label every progress bar with its actual denominator.F05, F18S-M
P1Move the theme trigger or prevent overlap with actions.F25S-M
P2Standardize cards, selected states, icons and typography.F04, F06, F07, F09M
P2Unify list filters, pagination, column priorities and row actions.F13, F14, F15M-L
P2Compact employee mobile rows and long administrative forms.F08, F11, F24M
P2Make hidden selections and bulk-save scope explicit.F17, F19S-M
P2Add sidebar disclosure cues and verify focus behavior.F03S-M
P3Add branded desktop/app icons; consider optional dashboard layout preferences only after usability testing.F07 and comparison reviewM

Recommended implementation order

First: header, search, copy and action hierarchy. Next: shared components applied to Employees, Tasks, Working Hours and Links. Then: reports, billing, mobile detail patterns and any optional dashboard customization.

Use visual snapshots plus workflow tests at each step. Keep timer start/stop, startup lock, entry correction, task reuse, permissions, client-specific linking and hour calculations unchanged unless a separate behavior change is requested.

Done means

  • One Tasks title; no icon/text overlap; one obvious primary action in the active editing context.
  • The last member of a long roster can be selected and saved without searching for the Save button.
  • Role restrictions, date scopes, half-day rules, history and timer confirmation survive the refresh.

13 / Comparison worksheet

Use the same tasks in each application

Complete this worksheet with current screenshots or recordings from accounts you are authorized to use. The CRM column is your baseline to measure; blank competitor cells mean not evaluated. Do not fill them with assumptions from marketing pages.

TaskCRM baseline to recordHanddyClockifyHubstaff
Start a normal work timerTime to choose project/client/task; clicks; whether Starting and Running are distinct.Not testedNot testedNot tested
Find one employee’s daily hoursClicks, filters, date certainty, readability and time to a correct answer.Not testedNot testedNot tested
Compare two teamsTime to understand worked vs required vs pending; ability to explain progress bars.Not testedNot testedNot tested
Change a group requirementTime to select team or people; scope clarity; confirmation; recovery from an error.Not testedNot testedNot tested
Correct a time entryEmployee selection, audit visibility, editable precision and review clarity.Not testedNot testedNot tested
Use a 390 px wide screenMain action reachability, table/detail readability, horizontal scroll and keyboard focus.Not testedNot testedNot tested

Record these observations

  • Screen size and browser zoom; user role; theme; number of employees/tasks; date range.
  • Seconds to finish, click count, wrong turns, help needed and whether the result was correct.
  • Can the user explain the next action, the selected scope and what the main number means?
  • Does the screen keep selections and unsaved input after an error or refresh?
  • For ClickUp, compare card selection, dashboard organization and list density rather than assuming the same desktop time-lock workflow.

Simple rating rubric for your own comparison

RatingMeaning
1User cannot complete the task without assistance.
2Task completes with major confusion or repeated wrong turns.
3Task completes with minor friction.
4Task is clear, efficient and recoverable after errors.
5Task is immediately understandable and remains efficient across roles and screen sizes.

These are proposed research measures, not scores awarded to any application in this report. Keep task results separate from visual preference: an attractive screen can still be slower to use.
